{{Short description|Genus of extinct bird}} {{Speciesbox | fossil_range = Middle [[Eocene]]
([[Lutetian]]), ~{{fossilrange|47.2}} | image = Masillastrix blattophaga (holotype, SMF-ME 11964).jpg | image_caption = Holotype under different preparation stages, including stomach contents in inset (A) | display_parents = 2 | genus = Masillastrix | parent_authority = [[Gerald Mayr|Mayr]] ''in'' Mayr et al., [[2026 in paleontology|2026]] | species = blattophaga | authority = Mayr ''in'' Mayr et al., 2026 }} '''''Masillastrix''''' ({{lit|Messel owl}}) is an [[extinct]] genus of [[Stem group|stem]]-[[owl]] known from the mid-[[Eocene]] ([[Lutetian]] age) [[Messel Pit]] of Germany. The genus contains a [[Monotypic taxon|single species]], '''''Masillastrix blattophaga''''', known from a nearly complete [[postcrania]]l skeleton preserved on a [[Compression fossil|slab and counterslab]]. This specimen is the first owl fossil with well-preserved feathers from the tail and wings. ''Masillastrix'' is the second owl fossil described from the Messel Pit, following ''[[Palaeoglaux artophoron]]''. The preserved stomach contents of the ''Masillastrix'' specimen reveal an [[iridescent]] [[cockroach]], representing both the first instance of an insect as a fossil bird's last meal and the only known instance of an owl—extinct or otherwise—preying on this type of cockroach. == Discovery and naming == The ''Masillastrix'' fossil material was discovered by Bruno Behr during an excavation in 2025 at outcrops of the [[Messel Formation]] near in [[Messel]], [[Darmstadt-Dieburg]], Germany. The specimen was taken to the [[Naturmuseum Senckenberg|Senckenberg Research Institute]] in [[Frankfurt]], where Behr [[Fossil preparation|prepared]] it, and it is now permanently [[Accession number (cultural property)|accessioned]] as specimen SMF-ME 11964. It consists of a nearly complete skeleton missing most of the skull and the tip of the left forelimb, flattened on two opposing [[Compression fossil|slabs]], designated as A and B. Extensive feather traces are preserved around the wings and tail, the first such occurrence in a fossil owl. In 2026, [[Gerald Mayr]] and colleagues [[Species description|described]] ''Masillastrix blattophaga'' as a new genus and species of early owl based on these fossil remains, designating SMF-ME 11964 as the [[holotype]] specimen. The [[Genus|generic name]], ''Masillastrix'', combines the [[Latin]] name for Messel, {{lang|la|Masilla}}, with the Latin {{lang|la|[[:wikt:strix#Latin|strī̆x]]}}, meaning {{gloss|owl}} (also the genus name of [[Strix (bird)|earless owls]]). The [[Specific name (zoology)|specific name]], ''blattophaga'', derives from ''[[Blatta]]'', a cockroach genus, and the [[Greek language|Greek]] word {{lang|grc|[[:wikt:φᾰγεῖν|φᾰγεῖν]]}} ({{lang|grc|phăgeîn}}), meaning {{gloss|to eat}}. ''Masillastrix'' is the second fossil owl named from the Messel Pit, following ''[[Palaeoglaux artophoron]]'' in 1992. == Description and palaeobiology == [[File:Messel Pit iridescent cockroach fossils.jpg|thumb|left|Stomach contents of the ''M. blattophaga'' holotype (E, F) compared to another iridescent Messel cockroach (G) and an extant specimen (H)]] The ''M. blattophaga'' holotype belongs to an immature individual, indicated by the furrowed texture on the surface of the large limb bones. The [[metatarsal]]s are fused, suggesting it had nearly reached its adult size, suggesting it was a [[Fledge|fledgling]] (capable of flight but still reliant on parental care). The [[humerus]] (upper arm bone) is proportionately smaller, and with a wider upper end, than in all [[Neontology|extant]] (living) owls, similar to ''[[Ypresiglaux]]''. The [[tarsometatarsus]] is short and robust, like in ''[[Minerva (bird)|Minerva]]''. The [[ungual]]s (claws) of the first and second toes of ''Masillastrix'' are notably larger than the unguals of the third and fourth toes, a feature characteristic of members of the family [[Protostrigidae]], but distinct from the coeval ''Palaeoglaux'' and extant owls. The preserved wing feather traces indicate that the [[primary feather]]s are proportionately short compared to extant owls (possibly related to its immature status). The outermost primary feather lacks any fraying; frayed edges are seen in most extant owls, and are an adaptation to sound reduction when flying. The tail feathers all have a similar length, contrasting with extant owls, where the tail is rounded. None of the wing or tail feathers exhibit the barred pattern seen in most modern owls. The remains of an [[iridescent]] cockroach (family [[Blaberidae]]) were identified within the preserved stomach contents of the ''M. blattophaga'' holotype. No other fossil birds have been identified with insect remains as their last meal. While some modern owls are [[insectivorous]], and at least one—the [[Akun eagle-owl]]—eats [[nocturnal]] cockroaches, no modern owls have been recorded eating iridescent cockroaches. Most modern cockroaches are nocturnal, though iridescent species are more frequently [[Diurnality|diurnal]] (active during daytime), suggesting ''Masillastrix'' was also diurnal. A diurnal ecology for this early owl is also supported by its robust, proportionately short wings and lack of frayed feathers, since long wings and frayed feathers are adaptations to nocturnal hunting in extant owls. == Classification == [[File:Eocene owls (fossil feet).jpg|thumb|Feet of ''Masillastrix'' (A–E) compared to other Eocene stem-owls]] To test the affinities and relationships of ''Masillastrix'', Mayr et al. (2026) included it in an updated version of the [[phylogenetic]] matrix of Mayr & Kitchener (2023). ''Masillastrix'' was recovered as part of the owl [[stem group]] (member of the [[Strigiformes]] outside of the smallest group including all modern owls), in an [[Polytomy|unresolved]] clade also including ''[[Minerva (bird)|Minerva]]'' and ''[[Oligostrix]]''.
